x:
Take a look at the recent book Sprint: http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/25814544-sprint?from_sear...

It details a creative process for developing concepts and testing them. Given that the book outlines a 5-day process that is tailored for product development teams, you might get a lot out of it for personal projects.

stt: Ask HN: What's the best book on modern UI/UX?
x:
I had the goal of learning UX basics in as little time as possible.

I took a 2 hour General Assembly course and found it incredibly useful - it sounds crazy but I feel like I learned 50% of what I needed to know about UX in just those 2 hours.

I asked some UX peeps what books they recommended and I purchased 2 and never read a single page (they were The Lean Startup by Eric Ries and Sprint by Google Ventures).

For web app UX, I found this 30 minute video extremely useful (great to see how a non-design person might make something, then how that same non-design person can change the primitive app they made into something very nice!).

Design for Non-Designers:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21byk2WWz3k

stt: Ask HN: What books helped you in your entrepreneurship journey?
x:
Sprint (product development and testing)

It left me with a more fundamental, "first principles" outlook on the 5 key stages of doing _anything_:

1. Understand

2. Explore

3. Decide

4. Prototype/Build

5. Test

So for example, when things often go wrong it's because a stage was skipped, done out of sequence, or extremely neglected.
